payload.rationale: The contract requires the NASA GISS unsmoothed LOTI for 2026 to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C, which is effectively the 2024 record (GISS reported 2024 at about 1.28°C above the 1951–1980 baseline; 2025 came in below that, roughly 1.2°C). So YES requires a new all-time record. Background considerations: 2024 was boosted by a strong 2023–24 El Niño; 2025 ranked second/third despite ENSO-neutral-to-La-Niña conditions, showing a high underlying baseline. 2026 began under weak La Niña conditions, which typically depress early-year global temperatures, and although several models projected El Niño development during 2026, El Niño's influence on the global annual mean lags by several months, so it would boost 2027 more than 2026. Pre-year forecasts (e.g., Met Office, Berkeley Earth-type outlooks) generally placed 2026 among the top few warmest years but with only a modest chance of a record. No 2026 observations were supplied, so I cannot condition on the ~8 months of data that exist as of the cutoff. Reasons this could be too high: La Niña-cooled early months plus GISS's 1.28 bar mean 2026 would need an unusually rapid warm surge; the record requires beating a strong-El-Niño year. Reasons this could be too low: the post-2023 step-up in baseline temperatures has persisted surprisingly, a rapidly developing strong El Niño in the second half of 2026 combined with low aerosols and high ocean heat content could push the annual mean past 1.28, and GISS often runs warmer than other datasets in recent years.
limitations: No 2026 monthly GISS data or ENSO observations supplied; estimate relies on general background knowledge up to early 2026.
Exact GISS 2025 annual value and any revisions to 2024 are recalled approximately.
Threshold sensitivity: outcome hinges on hundredths of a degree and GISS reporting precision.
